# Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/spinal-cord-stimulation-tms-and-tdcs-for-gait-and-motor-symptoms/

# Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.5.1 · generated 2026-11-27 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The rTMS review warns that small study numbers, heterogeneous medication state and disease severity, and uncontrolled protocol differences constrain generalizability and clinical recommendations; its subgroup results should not be treated as a validated optimal prescription. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12786542/
- [statement] A double-blind randomized trial of multitarget tDCS (abstract copyright 2021) enrolled seventy-seven participants with Parkinson disease and freezing; it did not improve the primary laboratory freezing-provoking test, although secondary self-reported freezing and daily step-count outcomes favored stimulation and a milder-freezing subgroup showed signals warranting further investigation. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34406695/
- [statement] The updated European evidence-based guidelines on rTMS (literature through the end of 2018; copyright 2019) assign Level B evidence (probable efficacy) to high-frequency rTMS of bilateral primary motor cortex regions for improving motor impairment in Parkinson's disease and to high-frequency rTMS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for improving depression in Parkinson's disease, and state that this does not mean the benefit inevitably reaches a level of clinical relevance. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31901449/
- [statement] The registry record for NCT06798844, a KU Leuven trial (design phase listed as PHASE2) of spinal cord stimulation for freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease, lists overall status ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING (status verified 2026-05), estimated enrollment 29 and estimated primary completion 2027-05. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06798844

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Terkelsen et al. reported improved Lower Body and Gait scores at twelve months, during an open extension rather than a continued sham-controlled comparison; the authors explicitly state that a placebo effect on open-phase patient-reported improvements cannot be excluded. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] A randomized double-blind SCS evaluation (abstract copyright 2025) was stopped for futility after eight implantations and seven completed blinded evaluations; active stimulation did not significantly improve Timed Up and Go or the other measured outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40172032/
- [statement] In the MicroBurst feasibility trial, twelve participants were randomized to six months of active stimulation or sham. The primary clinical PIGD endpoint was not met, although feasibility and safety endpoints were met. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/ · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w
- [statement] The blinded comparisons in the Carra 2025 and Terkelsen 2026 trials did not establish a significant gait benefit from their tested SCS protocols; these findings are protocol-specific and do not prove that every possible SCS approach is ineffective. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40172032/ · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/
- [statement] SCS implantation carries procedural risks: Terkelsen et al. reported four serious adverse events related to implantation, comprising dural puncture, two lead misplacements, and perioperative pain; dural puncture and lead misplacement required repeat surgery. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-68782-w · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/
- [statement] A randomized double-blind sham-controlled trial (abstract copyright 2019) allocated thirty patients with freezing of gait to ten sessions of real or sham 10 Hz rTMS over the supplementary motor area; ON-medication assessments showed improvements in freezing questionnaire, motor, and gait outcomes during follow-up through four weeks. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31689588/
- [statement] An rTMS meta-analysis of randomized trials searching through December 2024 included nineteen studies and 547 participants. It found benefits for freezing, gait speed and UPDRS-III, but not UPDRS total or TUG; publication-bias testing was positive for gait speed. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41517414/
- [statement] Liu et al. (2021) synthesized twenty-one tDCS studies involving 736 participants and concluded that evidence for motor improvement was insufficient; pooled UPDRS-III, Timed Up and Go, balance, and gait outcomes did not establish a motor benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8584149/
- [statement] The tDCS review reports headache, tingling, forehead burning, and a small number of first-degree burns in included studies; the authors reported no serious consequences from these events, so noninvasive stimulation should not be described as having no adverse effects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8584149/
- [statement] Implanted SCS delivers electrical stimulation through an epidural lead connected to a subcutaneous pulse generator; its use for Parkinsonian gait is distinct from its established pain indication. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12960713/
- [statement] rTMS has shown benefits for selected gait and motor outcomes in a randomized treadmill-training trial and a pooled analysis; benefit should be interpreted by outcome and stimulation protocol. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8470277/ · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41517414/
- [statement] In a randomized trial of fifty-one participants, twelve sessions of 1Hz or 25Hz rTMS before treadmill training improved fastest walking speed more than sham at one day and three months; this evaluates rTMS as a rehabilitation adjunct. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8470277/
- [statement] Evidence reviewed here does not establish reliable tDCS benefit for Parkinsonian motor function: a randomized freezing-of-gait trial missed its primary endpoint and a 2021 systematic review found insufficient motor-function evidence. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34406695/ · keywords: Spinal cord stimulation, TMS and tDCS for gait and motor symptoms · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8584149/
